title: When the Spark Fades
description: Motivation usually fades because the goal got vague, or stopped being yours. Here's how to check the why and make the target specific enough to chase.
excerpt: Check whose goal it is. Then make it specific enough to chase.

blocks.text: When motivation disappears, the instinct is to question your discipline. In practice, the problem is usually upstream of that. The goal got vague, or it stopped being yours. Both feel like laziness from the inside. Neither gets fixed by trying harder.

blocks.heading: Check whose goal it is
blocks.text: Some goals are inherited. A career someone else wanted for you. A body shape from an algorithm. A version of success you picked up at nineteen and never re-checked. You can force those for a while. You can't sustain them, because there's no honest answer to "why bother." Ask what you'd still want if nobody found out you achieved it. What survives that question is worth building on.

blocks.heading: Make it specific enough to chase
items: "Get fit" is a mood. "Three sessions a week: Monday, Wednesday, Saturday" is a target.
Name the next action, not the outcome. Outcomes aren't things you can do today.
Attach it to a time and a place, or it stays hypothetical.
Define done. Vague goals never finish. They only generate guilt.

blocks.heading: Expect the dip, plan for it
blocks.text: Every worthwhile pursuit has a middle stretch where the novelty is gone and the results haven't arrived. That's not a sign you chose wrong. It's the normal shape of the thing. Decide now what you'll do during that stretch. Deciding during it is how people quit.

items.q: What if I don't know what I want anymore?
items.a: Then stop building a five-year plan. Run a two-week experiment on one small target and see if you still care when it's specific. Clarity comes from contact, not from more thinking.

items.q: Is it okay to drop a goal?
items.a: Yes, if it fails the "whose goal is this" test. Quitting something that was never yours isn't failure. It's editing.
